title: list()
summary: A mutable, ordered sequence — the default collection, and a poor queue.
description: Backed by a contiguous array of references. That makes indexing and appending fast, and anything involving the *front* slow, because every later element has to shift.

parameters.name: iterable
parameters.description: Items to build the list from.

examples.title: Copying
examples.code:
a = [1, 2]
b = a[:]
b.append(3)
print(a, b)

real_world_usage: Almost every ordered collection: rows read from a file, results accumulated in a loop, a stack.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using a list as a queue with pop(0)
common_mistakes.fix: pop(0) is O(n), so draining is O(n^2). Use collections.deque.
That is O(n*m). Build a set once and test against it.

common_mistakes.mistake: A mutable default argument: def f(items=[])
common_mistakes.fix: The list is created once and shared between calls. Use None and create inside.
The index shifts and elements get skipped. Iterate a copy, or build a new list.

performance_notes: Index O(1); append amortised O(1); `in`, insert(0) and pop(0) all O(n). Those last three are the source of most accidental quadratic behaviour.
security_notes: Unbounded appends from untrusted input are a memory-exhaustion vector. Bound the size explicitly.
